question: Explain the State design pattern. How is it different from the Strategy pattern, given that both involve swapping in different behavior objects?

key_points: the State pattern represents an object's distinct internal states as separate classes, with the object's behavior changing as its current state object changes
state transitions are typically triggered by the states themselves (or the context), based on the object's own internal logic, as part of a state machine
the Strategy pattern swaps interchangeable algorithms/behaviors chosen externally by client code, generally without any notion of transitioning between them over time
structurally the two patterns look almost identical (a context holding a reference to an interchangeable object), but their intent differs: modeling a state machine versus selecting an algorithm
state pattern objects often know about and trigger transitions to other state objects; strategy objects usually don't know about other strategies at all
reference_solution.sample_answer: The State pattern represents an object's distinct internal states as separate classes, and the object's observable behavior changes as its current state object changes, with transitions between states typically triggered by the states themselves as part of an implicit state machine — like a TCP connection object behaving completely differently depending on whether its current state object represents 'listening', 'established', or 'closed'. question: Explain the Visitor design pattern and the double dispatch technique it relies on.

each element class implements an accept(visitor) method that calls back the appropriate visit method on the visitor for its own concrete type
this two-step call (element.accept(visitor) then visitor.visit(this)) is double dispatch: the actual method invoked depends on both the element's runtime type and the visitor's runtime type
standard single-dispatch OOP method calls only pick a method based on the receiver's runtime type, not a second argument's type too, which is exactly the gap double dispatch fills
trade-off: adding a new operation is easy (just a new visitor), but adding a new element class requires updating every existing visitor to handle it
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Visitor pattern lets you add new operations over a fixed set of element classes without modifying those classes themselves, by pulling each operation out into its own separate visitor object instead. Each element class implements an accept(visitor) method, which calls back the appropriate visit method on the visitor specifically for that element's own concrete type, and this two-step call — element.accept(visitor) followed by visitor.visit(this) — is exactly what's meant by double dispatch: the method that actually runs depends on both the element's runtime type and the visitor's runtime type together. This matters because standard single-dispatch OOP method calls only ever pick a method based on the single receiver object's runtime type, with no way to also dispatch based on a second argument's runtime type — double dispatch fills exactly that gap. The trade-off is that adding a brand-new operation is easy, just write a new visitor class, but adding a brand-new element class requires going back and updating every existing visitor to handle it.

question: Explain the Iterator design pattern. Why is it useful to decouple traversal logic from the collection being traversed?

key_points: the Iterator pattern provides a standard way (typically hasNext()/next() methods) to access a collection's elements sequentially without exposing its internal structure
client code can traverse different underlying data structures (array, linked list, tree) through the exact same uniform iterator interface
multiple independent iterators can traverse the same collection simultaneously without interfering with each other, unlike a single shared traversal position stored on the collection itself
lets the collection's internal representation change freely without breaking any client code that only ever depends on the iterator interface
this pattern is built directly into most modern languages' standard collection libraries and for-each style loops
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Iterator pattern provides a standard, uniform way, typically via hasNext() and next() methods, to access a collection's elements one at a time in sequence, without the client code needing to know anything about how that collection is actually implemented internally. This means client code can traverse a completely different underlying data structure, like an array, a linked list, or a tree, through the exact same iterator interface, and multiple independent iterators can traverse the same collection at the same time without interfering with each other, unlike if the traversal position were just stored as shared mutable state on the collection itself. It also means the collection's internal representation is free to change without breaking any client code, since that code only ever depends on the iterator interface, not the collection's internals — this is exactly why most modern languages bake this pattern directly into their standard collection libraries and for-each style loop syntax.

question: Explain the Composite design pattern. How does it let client code treat individual objects and groups of objects uniformly?

key_points: Composite defines a common interface shared by both individual ('leaf') objects and containers of objects ('composite')
a composite object holds a collection of children, which can themselves be either leaves or further composites, forming a tree structure
client code calling an operation on the common interface doesn't need to know or care whether it's talking to a single leaf or an entire subtree of composites
a composite's implementation of the shared operation typically just delegates the call recursively to each of its children
classic real-world example: a filesystem where files and folders share a common interface, letting an operation like 'calculate total size' work uniformly on either
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Composite pattern defines one common interface shared by both individual 'leaf' objects and 'composite' container objects that hold a collection of children, where those children can themselves be either more leaves or further nested composites, forming a tree. Client code calling an operation through that shared interface doesn't need to know or care whether it's actually talking to a single leaf object or an entire subtree of nested composites — it just calls the same method either way. A composite's own implementation of that shared operation typically just delegates the call recursively down to each of its children, letting the recursion naturally handle arbitrarily deep nesting. The classic real-world example is a filesystem, where files and folders both implement a shared interface, letting an operation like 'calculate total size' work identically whether you call it on a single file or an entire deeply-nested folder tree.

question: Explain the Proxy design pattern. Give an example of a use case for a protection proxy versus a virtual (lazy-loading) proxy.

key_points: a proxy implements the same interface as a real subject object, standing in for it and controlling access to it
client code interacts with the proxy exactly as if it were the real object, without needing to know a proxy is even involved
a virtual (lazy-loading) proxy delays creating or loading the expensive real object until it's actually genuinely needed
a protection proxy adds access control, checking permissions before allowing a call through to the real object
other proxy variants exist too, like a remote proxy standing in for an object that actually lives on a different machine/process
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Proxy pattern implements the exact same interface as some real subject object, standing in for it and controlling access to it, so client code interacts with the proxy exactly as if it were the real object, with no need to even know a proxy is involved at all. A virtual proxy, or lazy-loading proxy, uses this to delay actually creating or loading an expensive real object until it's genuinely needed for the first time — like a proxy standing in for a large image that only actually loads the full image data the first time it's rendered. A protection proxy instead uses the same structural idea to add access control in front of the real object, checking whether the caller actually has permission before letting the call through to the real object at all. Other proxy variants exist too, like a remote proxy standing in for an object that actually lives on a completely different machine or process, making a remote call look like a normal local method call to client code.

question: Explain the Flyweight design pattern. What problem does sharing common object state solve?

key_points: Flyweight addresses memory overhead when you need to create an enormous number of similar objects
it separates an object's state into 'intrinsic' state (shared, identical across many instances) and 'extrinsic' state (unique per instance, supplied externally)

a factory typically manages creating and reusing flyweight objects, returning an existing shared instance instead of creating a new one when the intrinsic state already matches

reference_solution.sample_answer: The Flyweight pattern addresses the memory overhead of needing to create an enormous number of similar objects, by splitting each object's state into 'intrinsic' state that's identical and shareable across many instances, and 'extrinsic' state that's genuinely unique to each individual instance and supplied from the outside when needed. The shared intrinsic state gets stored once in a single shared flyweight object, and every logical 'instance' just holds a reference to that shared object plus whatever small amount of its own extrinsic state it actually needs, dramatically cutting total memory use compared to fully duplicating everything per instance. A factory typically manages this, handing back an existing shared flyweight instance instead of creating a new one whenever the requested intrinsic state already matches one that exists. The classic example is rendering millions of characters in a text editor, where each character's font and glyph rendering data is identical and shared across every occurrence of that character, and only its position on the page is genuinely unique extrinsic state per occurrence.

question: Explain the Bridge design pattern. How does it decouple an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently?

This lets the abstraction hierarchy and the implementation hierarchy evolve and be extended completely independently — adding a new abstraction variant, or a new implementation variant, only ever requires one new class rather than one new class per combination of the two. generics let you write one class or method parameterized by a type, with the compiler enforcing type correctness for whatever specific type is used at each call site
this gives both code reuse and compile-time type safety simultaneously, rather than forcing a choice between the two
without generics and relying on an untyped base type instead, type mismatches are only caught at runtime via casting errors, not at compile time
generics also avoid the runtime cost of unnecessary casting between the untyped base type and the actual concrete type being used
reference_solution.sample_answer: Without generics, writing a single reusable collection or algorithm that works across many different types forces a choice: either duplicate the same code separately for every type you need to support, or write it once against a common untyped base type, like Object, which loses compile-time type safety since anything could technically be stored or passed in. Generics let you write one class or method parameterized by a type variable, and the compiler then enforces type correctness for whatever specific type is actually used at each individual call site, giving you both code reuse and genuine compile-time type safety at the same time, instead of having to pick just one. question: What is type erasure in Java's generics implementation, and what practical limitations does it cause?

key_points: Java's generics are checked for type correctness at compile time, but the actual generic type parameter information is erased and not retained in the compiled bytecode at runtime
at runtime, a generic class effectively only knows it's working with its erased raw type (often Object, or the parameter's upper bound), not the specific type argument that was used at that call site
practical limitation: you can't reliably check an object's specific generic type argument at runtime (e.g. distinguishing a List<String> from a List<Integer> via reflection at runtime)
you also generally can't create an array of a generic type parameter directly, since the runtime doesn't retain enough information to do so safely
this was a deliberate backward-compatibility design choice, letting generic code interoperate with code compiled before generics existed
reference_solution.sample_answer: Java's generics are fully checked for type correctness at compile time, but the actual specific generic type parameter used is erased and not retained at all in the compiled bytecode — at runtime, a generic class effectively only knows about its erased raw type, often just Object or the parameter's declared upper bound, rather than the concrete type argument that was actually used at any given call site. The practical limitation this causes is that you can't reliably inspect an object's specific generic type argument at runtime — there's no way to distinguish a List<String> instance from a List<Integer> instance via reflection at runtime, since that distinction simply doesn't exist anymore once erasure happens. It also generally prevents you from directly creating an array of a generic type parameter, since the runtime doesn't retain enough type information to do that safely. This was a deliberate backward-compatibility design choice specifically so that newly-written generic code could still interoperate cleanly with code that had been compiled before generics were even introduced to the language.

question: What is operator overloading, and what are its pros and cons as a language feature?

key_points: operator overloading lets a class define custom behavior for built-in operators (like +, ==, <) when applied to its own instances
used well, it can make code involving custom types (e.g. a Vector or Money class) read naturally, close to how it reads for built-in numeric types
used poorly, it can make an operator do something surprising or unrelated to its conventional meaning, making code harder to reason about at a glance
some languages deliberately restrict or omit operator overloading specifically to avoid this readability risk, favoring explicit named methods instead
a common convention is that overloaded operators should behave consistently with the operator's normal, expected semantics (e.g. + should still feel like 'combining' two things)
reference_solution.sample_answer: Operator overloading lets a class define custom behavior for built-in operators like +, ==, or < when they're applied to instances of that class, rather than those operators only ever working on primitive numeric types. Used well, this can make code involving a custom type, like a Vector or Money class, read naturally and closely to how the equivalent code reads for a built-in numeric type, which is a genuine readability win. Used poorly, though, it can make an operator do something completely surprising or unrelated to its conventional meaning, which makes code much harder to reason about at a glance, since readers can no longer assume + always means straightforward addition-like combination. Some languages deliberately restrict or entirely omit operator overloading specifically to avoid this readability risk, preferring explicit named methods instead — and even in languages that do support it, the common convention is that an overloaded operator should still behave consistently with what that operator conventionally means, so + should still feel like 'combining' two things, not something unrelated.

question: What is a fluent interface, and how does method chaining make it possible?

reference_solution.sample_answer: A fluent interface is an API design style meant to read almost like natural language, typically achieved through a chain of method calls rather than a series of separate statements each assigning to a variable. Method chaining is what makes this possible: each method in the chain returns the object itself, or a related builder object, so the next method in the chain can be called directly on whatever was just returned, letting the whole sequence be written as one continuous expression. This is commonly used for builder-style object construction or query-building APIs, where each call incrementally refines the final configuration or result being built up. It genuinely improves readability for this specific kind of incremental configuration, but it can cost some debuggability, since a single failing call somewhere in a long chain can be harder to isolate and inspect than if each step were written as its own separate statement with its own intermediate variable.

question: Compare constructor injection, setter injection, and interface injection as ways of doing dependency injection. What are the trade-offs of each?

key_points: constructor injection passes dependencies through the constructor, making them mandatory and guaranteeing the object is never in an incompletely-configured state
setter injection passes dependencies through setter methods after construction, allowing optional dependencies but risking a window where the object exists without all dependencies set yet

interface injection requires a dependency-providing interface that the object implements, with the injector calling a specific method to supply the dependency, giving the framework more control over exactly when injection happens
constructor injection is generally preferred by default for required dependencies, since it makes them explicit and enforced at object creation time
setter injection is more appropriate for genuinely optional dependencies or when a dependency might need to change after construction
reference_solution.sample_answer: Constructor injection passes an object's dependencies in through its constructor, which makes them mandatory and guarantees the object is never in a partially-configured, invalid state at any point after construction completes. Setter injection instead passes dependencies through setter methods called after construction, which allows for genuinely optional dependencies, but does risk a brief window where the object technically exists but doesn't yet have all its dependencies set, if something calls a method on it too early. Interface injection requires the object to implement a specific dependency-providing interface, with the injecting framework calling a designated method to supply the dependency, giving the framework itself more explicit control over exactly when and how injection happens, though it's less commonly used today than the other two approaches. In general, I'd default to constructor injection for anything the object genuinely requires to function correctly, since it makes those dependencies explicit and enforced right at creation time, and reach for setter injection specifically for dependencies that are truly optional or might need to be swapped out after construction.

question: What's the practical difference between an abstract method and a virtual method?

key_points: an abstract method has no implementation at all in the declaring class and must be overridden by any concrete subclass before that subclass can be instantiated
a virtual method does have a default implementation in the declaring class, but explicitly allows subclasses to override it with their own behavior if they choose to

reference_solution.sample_answer: An abstract method has no implementation at all in the class that declares it, and any concrete subclass is required to provide an actual implementation before it can be instantiated at all — a class containing any abstract method is itself necessarily abstract and can't be instantiated directly. A virtual method, by contrast, does have a default implementation already provided in the declaring class, but is explicitly marked as overridable, so subclasses can choose to override it with their own behavior if they need something different, while a class containing only virtual methods can still be instantiated directly and will just use those default implementations wherever no subclass has chosen to override them. The choice signals real intent to subclass authors: an abstract method forces every subclass to actually think about and provide meaningful behavior for it, while a virtual method offers a sensible, usable default while still leaving the door open for customization.

question: What is object pooling, and when would you use it instead of just creating and destroying objects as needed?

key_points: object pooling maintains a pre-allocated set of reusable objects, handed out to callers and returned to the pool when done, instead of constructing and destroying a fresh one each time
useful specifically when object construction/destruction is genuinely expensive relative to how frequently objects are needed and released
reduces both allocation overhead and garbage collection pressure in managed-memory languages, since fewer objects are being churned through creation and collection
requires objects to be properly reset to a clean state before being reused, or stale state from a previous use can leak into the next user
unnecessary for cheap-to-create objects, where the pool's own bookkeeping overhead can outweigh any benefit
reference_solution.sample_answer: Object pooling maintains a pre-allocated set of reusable objects that get handed out to callers on request and returned to the pool when the caller is done with them, instead of constructing a brand-new object and letting the old one get destroyed or garbage-collected every single time one is needed. This is useful specifically when object construction or destruction is genuinely expensive relative to how often objects actually get requested and released, like frequently-created network connections or particles in a game engine's rendering loop. In a managed-memory language, it also meaningfully reduces garbage collection pressure, since far fewer objects are being churned through allocation and collection over time. The important correctness requirement is that objects must be properly reset back to a clean state before being handed out again, or stale state from a previous use can leak into the next caller in a confusing way — and it's genuinely unnecessary for objects that are cheap to create in the first place, where the pool's own bookkeeping overhead could actually outweigh any benefit.

question: In domain-driven design terms, what's the difference between a value object and an entity?

key_points: an entity has a distinct identity that persists over time, tracked independently of its current attribute values (e.g. a customer with a stable ID, even if their name or address changes)

a value object has no meaningful identity of its own; it's defined entirely by the combination of its attribute values, and two value objects with identical attributes are considered equal and interchangeable

entities are typically compared by identity (same ID means same entity, even with different current attributes); value objects are typically compared by value (same attributes means equal, regardless of separate instances)
value objects are naturally good candidates for immutability, since 'changing' one conceptually just means replacing it with a different value object entirely
a classic value object example is a Money amount or an Address; a classic entity example is a Customer or an Order
reference_solution.sample_answer: An entity has a distinct identity that persists over time and is tracked independently of its current attribute values — a customer is still the same customer, tracked by a stable ID, even after their name or address changes. A value object has no meaningful identity of its own at all; it's defined entirely by the combination of its actual attribute values, so two separate value object instances with identical attributes are considered fully equal and interchangeable, regardless of being distinct objects in memory. This means entities are typically compared by identity — same ID means the same entity, even with different current attribute values — while value objects are compared by value, where matching attributes means equality regardless of instance identity. Value objects are naturally good candidates for immutability, since conceptually 'changing' one just means replacing it entirely with a different value object rather than mutating something with its own persistent identity — a classic example is a Money amount or an Address, contrasted with a Customer or an Order, which are classic entities.

question: In domain-driven design, what is an aggregate root, and what responsibility does it have for the objects inside its aggregate?

the aggregate root is the single designated entity through which all external access to the aggregate's internals must go

reference_solution.sample_answer: An aggregate is a cluster of related entities and value objects that should be treated together as one consistency boundary for a given business operation — for example, an Order along with its OrderLine items might form one aggregate. The aggregate root is the single designated entity through which all external access to anything inside that aggregate must go; external code isn't allowed to hold a direct reference to, or directly modify, an internal object like an individual OrderLine except by calling methods on the root itself. This matters because it lets the root enforce business invariants consistently across the entire aggregate, since every possible mutation is forced to pass through it rather than being able to bypass its rules by reaching into an internal object directly. Aggregates are also typically the natural boundary a repository uses for loading, saving, and enforcing transactional consistency, rather than loading and saving the individual internal objects separately and independently.

question: What's a common mistake developers make when confusing an 'is-a' relationship with a 'has-a' relationship in class design?

'has-a' should be modeled with composition: an object contains or uses another object as a part or capability, without being a specialized version of it
a classic mistake is inheriting from a class purely to reuse its implementation code, even though the new class isn't genuinely a specialized version of the base conceptually
this produces a class hierarchy that violates Liskov Substitution or just doesn't make logical sense, since the 'is-a' relationship being modeled isn't actually true in the real domain
the fix is usually to switch to composition: having the new class hold an instance of the other class as a field, and delegate to it, rather than inheriting from it
reference_solution.sample_answer: A common mistake is inheriting from a class purely to reuse its existing implementation code, even though the new class isn't genuinely a more specific kind of that base class conceptually — the classic overused example is a Stack class inheriting from a List class just to reuse the List's underlying storage logic, when a Stack isn't truly 'a kind of' List in a substitutability sense; it just happens to need similar internal storage. This produces a hierarchy that violates the Liskov Substitution Principle, or just doesn't logically make sense in the domain, since the 'is-a' relationship being claimed isn't actually true. The fix is almost always to switch to composition instead: have the new class hold an instance of the other class as a private field and delegate to it for the specific behavior it actually needs, rather than inheriting the entire public interface and behavior of a class it isn't genuinely a specialized version of.

question: What's the design difference between checked and unchecked exceptions, and what trade-off does a language make by choosing one approach over the other?

key_points: checked exceptions must be either caught or explicitly declared as thrown by a method, enforced by the compiler; unchecked exceptions have no such compile-time requirement
checked exceptions force callers to consciously acknowledge and handle a specific failure mode, which can genuinely improve reliability for expected, recoverable failure conditions
in practice, checked exceptions can also lead to boilerplate try/catch blocks or overly broad catches just to satisfy the compiler, sometimes without genuinely handling the error meaningfully
unchecked exceptions give more flexibility and less boilerplate, but rely entirely on documentation and convention to inform callers about what a method might throw
different mainstream languages have made genuinely different design choices here (e.g. Java has both, C# only has unchecked), reflecting this real trade-off rather than one clearly superior answer
reference_solution.sample_answer: Checked exceptions must be either caught or explicitly declared as thrown in a method's signature, enforced by the compiler, while unchecked exceptions have no such compile-time requirement at all and can be thrown or propagate freely with no compiler-enforced acknowledgment. Checked exceptions force callers to consciously deal with a specific, expected failure mode, which can genuinely improve reliability for conditions that are truly expected and recoverable, like a file not being found. In practice, though, this can backfire into boilerplate try/catch blocks, or overly broad catches written purely to satisfy the compiler rather than to genuinely and meaningfully handle the error. Unchecked exceptions trade that compiler enforcement away for more flexibility and less boilerplate, relying entirely on documentation and convention to actually inform callers about what a method might throw. Different mainstream languages have made genuinely different choices here — Java supports both checked and unchecked exceptions, while C# only has unchecked exceptions — reflecting that this is a real design trade-off, not a settled question with one clearly superior answer.

question: When designing a custom exception hierarchy, how would you decide when a caller should catch and handle an exception locally versus let it propagate up?

key_points: catch and handle locally only when the current code actually has enough context to meaningfully recover or take a specific corrective action
if the current code can't do anything genuinely useful with the exception besides logging and re-throwing, it's usually better to let it propagate to a layer that can actually act on it
a custom exception hierarchy should distinguish exceptions by how a caller should reasonably respond, not just by their internal implementation cause
catching an overly broad exception type (like a generic base Exception) risks silently swallowing unrelated, unexpected failures that should have propagated and been surfaced

exceptions crossing an architectural boundary (e.g. into an API response) often need to be translated into a different, more caller-appropriate exception type rather than leaking internal implementation details directly
reference_solution.sample_answer: I'd only catch and handle an exception locally where the current code genuinely has enough context to take a specific, meaningful corrective action, like retrying a transient failure or falling back to a sensible default value. If the current code can't actually do anything useful besides logging and re-throwing the exact same exception, I'd generally just let it propagate up to a layer that actually has the context to decide what to do, rather than adding a catch block that doesn't meaningfully change anything. When designing the exception hierarchy itself, I'd organize exception types by how a caller should reasonably respond to them, not just by their internal implementation cause, so a caller can catch a meaningful category rather than an unrelated grab-bag of exceptions that happen to share an internal cause. I'd also be careful about catching an overly broad exception type like a generic base Exception, since that risks silently swallowing genuinely unexpected failures that should have propagated and been visibly surfaced, and I'd translate exceptions crossing an architectural boundary, like into an API response, into a different, more caller-appropriate type instead of leaking internal implementation details directly.

question: What is the Repository design pattern, and why is it used to abstract data access away from the rest of an application's business logic?

key_points: a repository presents a collection-like interface (add, get, remove, query) for a domain object, hiding exactly how and where the underlying data is actually stored
business logic depends only on the repository's interface, not on any specific database technology or query language details
this makes it much easier to swap the underlying storage technology, or to substitute a fake/in-memory repository implementation for fast, isolated unit testing
without this abstraction, database-specific query code tends to leak directly into business logic, coupling the two together tightly
a repository is usually scoped to one aggregate/domain concept, not a generic one-size-fits-all data access layer for the entire database
reference_solution.sample_answer: A repository presents a collection-like interface — think add, get, remove, and query methods — for working with a specific domain object, while hiding exactly how and where the underlying data actually gets stored, whether that's a relational database, a document store, or something else entirely. Business logic then only ever depends on that repository's interface, with no direct knowledge of any specific database technology or query language details baked into it. This makes it much easier to later swap the underlying storage technology without touching business logic at all, and just as importantly, makes it easy to substitute a fake, in-memory repository implementation during unit testing, letting tests run fast and in isolation without needing an actual database. Without this abstraction, database-specific query code tends to leak directly into business logic scattered throughout the codebase, tightly coupling the two together in a way that's hard to untangle later — and a repository is typically scoped to one specific aggregate or domain concept, rather than being one generic, do-everything data access layer for the whole database.

reference_solution.sample_answer: A Unit of Work tracks a set of changes made across one or more repositories during a single business operation, and it exposes a single commit operation that persists all of those tracked changes together, typically wrapped in one underlying database transaction. Without it, saving each repository's changes separately risks ending up in a partial, inconsistent state if one repository's save succeeds but a related save that should have happened alongside it fails partway through. The Unit of Work is what actually decides when changes get flushed to the database at all, which lets business logic freely modify several related objects across potentially multiple repositories and only worry about calling commit once, at the very end of the operation. Both patterns achieve this specifically by relying on polymorphism through a stable interface or base class, rather than a chain of conditional branches like a big switch statement, which is exactly the kind of code you'd otherwise have to keep editing every single time a new case needs to be added — precisely what OCP says to avoid.

the second check inside the lock is necessary because multiple threads could have passed the first check simultaneously before any of them acquired the lock

This whole pattern trades a small amount of extra implementation complexity specifically for avoiding lock overhead on every single call made after the instance has already been safely created.

question: What are the three classic categories of Gang of Four design patterns (creational, structural, behavioral), and what does each category address?

key_points: creational patterns address how objects are constructed, hiding or flexibly handling the exact instantiation logic (e.g. Factory Method, Builder, Singleton, Prototype)

structural patterns address how classes and objects are composed together into larger structures while keeping them flexible and efficient (e.g. Adapter, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Bridge, Flyweight)

behavioral patterns address how objects interact and distribute responsibility for behavior among each other (e.g. Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template Method, Visitor, Chain of Responsibility, Mediator, Iterator, Memento)
the categorization is a useful organizing lens for recognizing which kind of design problem you're actually facing, rather than a strict, unambiguous classification every pattern fits perfectly into
some patterns arguably straddle categories somewhat, but the three-way split still helps orient which family of solutions to consider first for a given problem
reference_solution.sample_answer: Creational patterns address how objects actually get constructed, hiding or flexibly handling the specific instantiation logic — this includes patterns like Factory Method, Builder, Singleton, and Prototype. Structural patterns address how classes and objects are composed together into larger structures while keeping that composition flexible and efficient, including patterns like Adapter, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Bridge, and Flyweight. Behavioral patterns address how objects actually interact with each other and how responsibility for behavior gets distributed among them, including patterns like Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template Method, Visitor, Chain of Responsibility, Mediator, Iterator, and Memento. This three-way categorization is really a useful organizing lens for recognizing what kind of design problem you're actually facing, rather than a perfectly strict classification that every single pattern fits into unambiguously — some patterns arguably touch more than one category somewhat — but the split still helps orient which broad family of solutions to consider first for a given problem.

question: You're reviewing a class hierarchy where a SavingsAccount subclass overrides withdraw() to throw an exception whenever the withdrawal would violate a minimum balance rule, but the base Account class's withdraw() never throws under any circumstances. Does this violate a SOLID principle, and if so, which one?

key_points: this violates the Liskov Substitution Principle, since SavingsAccount can no longer be safely substituted everywhere an Account is expected
existing code written against the base Account type has no reason to wrap withdraw() calls in a try/catch, since the base contract never promised an exception could occur
when that code is handed a SavingsAccount instead, it can crash unexpectedly on an exception it was never told to expect, purely because of this new failure mode introduced only in the subclass

the fix isn't to avoid ever adding new business rules in a subclass, but to make the new failure mode part of the base contract instead, e.g. having the base class's method signature/contract also account for a possible failure, or return an explicit result the caller must check
this is a concrete instance of LSP being violated through exception behavior rather than a mismatched method signature or return type
reference_solution.sample_answer: Yes, this violates the Liskov Substitution Principle. SavingsAccount is supposed to be usable everywhere an Account is expected, but existing code written against the base Account type has no reason to wrap calls to withdraw() in a try/catch, since the base class's contract never promised that any exception could occur there at all. If that same existing code is handed a SavingsAccount instead of a plain Account, it can now crash unexpectedly on an exception it was never told to expect, purely because of a new failure mode introduced only in this specific subclass. The fix isn't to avoid ever adding legitimate new business rules like a minimum balance check in a subclass — that's a perfectly reasonable rule to want — but to make that possible failure part of the base contract itself, for instance by having the base Account class's withdraw() method also declare that it can fail, or by returning an explicit success/failure result that every caller is already expected to check, rather than silently introducing a new, undeclared exception only in the subclass.
